title: Caches keep useful copies
summary: Save a copy of a repeated answer in a cache. Trace a hit, a miss, and expiry, then decide which data can safely be a little old.
introduction: A librarian keeps a note of a popular book's description beside the desk. Reading the note is quicker than looking up the record again. A cache is a similar shortcut, but its note can become out of date.
learningObjectives: Explain cache hits, misses, and expiry
Trace a cache-aside read with a tiny time model
Choose which facts need a fresh authoritative check

blocks.text: A **cache** keeps a copy that is quick to reach. The main database remains the **source of truth**: the place where the official record is kept.
A **hit** finds a usable cached answer. A **miss** does not, so the app reads the main record and saves a copy. This pattern is called **cache aside** because the app manages the extra copy.
A **time to live**, or **TTL**, says how long a cached item may be reused before it expires. Expiry limits one kind of staleness; it does not make the copy update as soon as the original changes.

items: At time 0, the cache is empty. Read the current title and keep it until time 10.
At time 5, reuse that cached title. This is a hit.
Change the source title. At time 6, the saved copy is still old.
At time 10, the saved copy expires. Read and cache the new title.

blocks.text: This small JavaScript model runs in the playground. Its numbers and events are chosen for learning. It does not create servers or measure a real service.

blocks.alt: A fresh cache copy can answer a read. A missing or old copy sends the service to the database, then the cache is refreshed.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows a read. Changing or borrowing a book needs separate rules to keep saved copies from being treated as current truth.

blocks.text: The value at time 6 is old even though the cache is working as designed. Decide whether that delay is acceptable for the fact you are showing.

When a book changes, the app can remove or refresh its cached entry. This is **invalidation**. Real systems must also handle two readers and writers racing; a simple remove-after-write rule alone can still leave an old copy in some races.

rows: More reuse and fewer database reads
People may see an old answer for longer
More misses send work to the database
Helps prevent lending an unavailable copy
The safe update needs the main record and transaction rules

blocks.text: If the cache goes down, the app may read the main database, but it must avoid flooding that database. Limits and graceful errors may be safer than unlimited fallback requests.

When a popular key expires, many readers may fetch it together. This is a cache stampede. Combining those fetches, refreshing early, or spreading expiry times can help. Never put private user results under a shared public key.

items: Change the TTL from 10 to 4. Predict the output at time 5.
It becomes a miss, because the first item expired at time 4. It still reads Moon Book because the source changes after that call.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not use an old cached availability count as permission to lend a book. Recheck and update the official record safely.
